Title: Rome in World Time, Part 10: The Fall of the West (AD 395–480)

Summary: In 85 years the western Roman Empire went from the most powerful state in Europe to a collection of Gothic, Vandal, Frankish and Burgundian kingdoms. Rome was sacked twice, Britain was abandoned, Africa's grain was lost to the Vandals, Attila's Huns invaded Gaul and Italy, and in 476 a Germanic general sent the last emperor in Italy into retirement. Meanwhile, the Northern Wei unified northern China in the same year Carthage fell, Huns attacked Gupta India as well, and Armenians fought Persia in the same weeks as the Catalaunian Plains.

---

"The fall of Rome" is one of the most argued-over topics in history. Was it murder by barbarians, suicide by civil war, or a slow transformation? This post sticks to what happened, decade by decade. One thing is clear from the timeline: the West never lost a single decisive battle. It bled out through a long series of revolts, usurpations, lost provinces and lost tax revenue.

## The two halves part ways (395–410)

After Theodosius died, the boy emperors **Arcadius** (East, at Constantinople) and **Honorius** (West) were controlled by their ministers. In the West that was **Stilicho**, a general of Vandal descent.

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 395–397 | **Alaric** and his Goths revolt and plunder Greece |
| **397–398** | **Gildo**, the Roman commander in Africa, switches loyalty to the East and cuts off Rome's grain supply. He is defeated by an army led by his own brother |
| 399–400 | **Tribigild** revolts in Anatolia; the Gothic general **Gainas** briefly controls Constantinople until the population rises and massacres thousands of Goths (July 400) |
| 401–402 | Alaric invades Italy; Stilicho fights him at **Pollentia** (Easter 402) and Verona |
| 402 | Honorius moves the western capital to marsh-protected **Ravenna** |
| 405–406 | **Radagaisus** invades Italy with a huge Gothic force; Stilicho destroys it at Faesulae |
| 31 Dec 406 | **Vandals, Alans and Suebi cross the Rhine** into Gaul (the date is traditional) |
| **406–407** | The army in **Britain** proclaims three emperors in a row: Marcus, Gratian and **Constantine III**, who crosses to Gaul |
| 408 | Honorius has Stilicho executed (22 August). Roman troops massacre the families of barbarian soldiers in Italy; thousands of those soldiers join Alaric |
| 408–409 | Alaric besieges Rome twice and makes the senator Priscus Attalus a puppet emperor |
| 409 | The Vandals, Alans and Suebi cross into **Spain**. In **Britain and Armorica** (Brittany), the locals expel Roman officials (Zosimus) |
| **24 Aug 410** | **Alaric sacks Rome**, the first time a foreign enemy has taken the city in 800 years. Three days of looting. Alaric dies weeks later in southern Italy |
| c. 410 | Honorius reportedly tells the British cities to see to their own defence. Roman Britain ends |

## Losing the provinces (410–450)

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 411 | Constantine III surrenders and is executed. Another usurper, **Jovinus**, appears on the Rhine (411–413) |
| 413 | **Heraclian**, governor of Africa, revolts and sails on Italy; executed |
| 413–426 | **Augustine** writes *The City of God*, partly to answer pagans who blamed Christianity for the sack |
| March 415 | The philosopher **Hypatia** is murdered by a Christian mob in Alexandria |
| 418 | The Visigoths are settled in **Aquitaine**, with their capital at Toulouse |
| 423–425 | After Honorius dies, a civil servant named **John** takes the throne; the East installs **Valentinian III**, aged six, with his mother **Galla Placidia** as regent |
| 429 | The **Vandals** under **Gaiseric** cross from Spain to Africa |
| 430 | Augustine dies (28 August) during the Vandal siege of Hippo |
| 435–437 | **Bagaudae** revolt in Gaul under Tibatto |
| 436–437 | Aetius' Hun allies destroy the **Burgundian** kingdom at Worms (the root of the *Nibelungenlied*) |
| **19 Oct 439** | The Vandals take **Carthage**. The West loses its richest provinces and its grain supply. Gaiseric builds a fleet |
| 441–447 | **Attila** and Bleda ravage the Balkans; the East pays heavy tribute |
| 447 | An earthquake topples Constantinople's walls during a Hun invasion; they are rebuilt in about two months |
| c. 446 | The Britons appeal to Aetius for help ("the groans of the Britons"), according to Gildas; none comes |
| c. 449 (trad.) | Traditional date of the **Anglo-Saxon** arrival under Hengist and Horsa |

## Attila (450–454)

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 450 | Valentinian's sister **Honoria**, to escape an arranged marriage, sends her ring to Attila, who claims her as his bride with half the western empire as dowry |
| 451 | Attila invades Gaul |
| **June 451** | **Battle of the Catalaunian Plains**: **Aetius**, with Visigoths, Franks and others, stops Attila. The Visigothic king Theodoric I dies in the battle |
| 451 | **Council of Chalcedon** defines Christ's nature; Egyptian and Syrian churches reject it, a split that still exists |
| 452 | Attila invades Italy and destroys **Aquileia** (refugees to the lagoons are part of Venice's founding legend). Pope **Leo I** meets him; Attila withdraws, also because of plague and famine in his army |
| 453 | Attila dies on his wedding night, apparently of a burst blood vessel |
| 454 | At the **Battle of Nedao** the Hun empire's subject peoples revolt and destroy it |
| 21 Sep 454 | Valentinian III personally kills **Aetius**, his best general, in the palace |

## The last emperors of the West (455–480)

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 16 Mar 455 | Two of Aetius' bodyguards kill **Valentinian III** |
| **June 455** | The **Vandals sack Rome** for two weeks, carrying off the empress and the treasures of the Jerusalem Temple. The emperor **Petronius Maximus** is killed by a mob while fleeing |
| 455–456 | **Avitus**, a Gallic noble backed by the Visigoths, is emperor; deposed by the general **Ricimer** |
| 457–461 | **Majorian**, the last capable western emperor, wins back much of Gaul, but his invasion fleet is destroyed at Cartagena in 460. Ricimer has him executed |
| 461–465 | Libius Severus, Ricimer's puppet |
| 467–472 | **Anthemius**, sent from the East |
| **468** | **Cape Bon**: a huge joint East–West fleet (over 1,000 ships) against the Vandals is destroyed by fire ships. The last real chance to save the West |
| 472 | Ricimer besieges and sacks Rome in a civil war with Anthemius; Anthemius is killed; Ricimer dies weeks later |
| 472–474 | Olybrius, then Glycerius |
| 474–475 | **Julius Nepos**, from Dalmatia |
| 475 | His general **Orestes** revolts and makes his own son, **Romulus "Augustulus,"** emperor |
| **4 Sep 476** | **Odoacer**, leader of the Germanic troops in Italy, kills Orestes and retires Romulus to a villa near Naples. He sends the imperial regalia to Constantinople, saying the West needs no emperor of its own |
| 480 | Julius Nepos, still recognised in the East and Dalmatia, is murdered. Some historians prefer 480 as the true end of the western line |

### In the East, meanwhile

Constantinople survived partly because of its walls (the **Theodosian Walls**, built around 413), its richer and more urban provinces, and luck: Attila and the Goths turned west. It had its own crises: the Gainas affair (400), Hun tribute, the powerful general **Aspar** (murdered 471), and the usurpation of **Basiliscus** (475–476).

## Things you might not have known happened at the same time

**Huns at both ends.** Attila's empire collapsed in 453–454, and around 455 the Gupta emperor Skandagupta was beating back "Huna" invaders in India. Whether these were the same people is debated, but steppe confederations were pressing on settled empires from Gaul to the Ganges in the same decade.

**439: one empire splits, another unifies.** The Vandal capture of Carthage was the moment the West lost its economic heart. That same year the Northern Wei finished conquering the last rival state in northern China. Unlike the Vandals, the Tuoba rulers of Wei went on to adopt Chinese ways so completely that they later banned their own language at court.

**Two battles for faith and freedom in 451.** Armenians fought the Persian army at Avarayr in late spring 451. A few weeks later Aetius fought Attila in Gaul. Both battles are national legends today: Avarayr in Armenia and the Catalaunian Plains in France.

**Rome fell, but Constantinople was the bigger city.** By the mid-400s, Constantinople probably had more people than Rome. The eastern half was richer, and it did not "fall" for nearly another thousand years. That is the subject of the last two posts.

**Most people in 476 did not notice.** Odoacer kept the Senate, Roman law and the Roman administration. Contemporaries did not write that "the Roman Empire fell" that year. The idea of 476 as the end came mostly later, from the sixth-century writer Marcellinus Comes and then from modern historians.

## What comes next

Part 11: the Roman Empire continues in the East. Justinian reconquers Africa and Italy, plague strikes, Heraclius saves the empire from Persia only to lose half of it to the Arabs, and Basil II restores Roman power. Meanwhile Tang China, the Islamic caliphates, Charlemagne and the Maya rise and fall.

## Sources and notes

- Zosimus, *New History*, Books 5–6 (to 410).
- Olympiodorus of Thebes (fragments), Priscus of Panium (fragments, including his visit to Attila's court in 449).
- Jordanes, *Getica* (the Goths and the Catalaunian Plains), Hydatius, *Chronicle* (Spain).
- Orosius, *Seven Books of History against the Pagans*; Augustine, *The City of God*.
- Gildas, *On the Ruin of Britain*.
- Peter Heather, *The Fall of the Roman Empire* (2005); Bryan Ward-Perkins, *The Fall of Rome and the End of Civilization* (2005); Guy Halsall, *Barbarian Migrations and the Roman West* (2007), for different views.
- Elishe, *History of Vardan and the Armenian War*, for Avarayr.
- Overview: [Sack of Rome (410) (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Rome_%28410%29), [Battle of the Catalaunian Plains (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Catalaunian_Plains), [Fall of the Western Roman Empire (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_the_Western_Roman_Empire).

**Flags:** The Rhine crossing is traditionally dated 31 December 406, but some historians argue for 405. The "Rescript of Honorius" may refer to Bruttium in Italy, not Britain. The Hengist and Horsa date and St Patrick's dates are traditional. The exact date of the Catalaunian Plains (20 June is traditional) and of Avarayr (26 May or 2 June) varies by source. The link between the Huns of Europe and the Hunas of India is debated. The Nalanda foundation date is approximate.
